extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, communicators, PR researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Use organizational linkage concepts and a situational theory of publics to identify, classify, and prioritize the publics an organization must communicate with; determine appropriate PR objectives and programs for each. Emphasizes diagnosing consequences, boundary roles, and measuring problem recognition, constraint recognition, and involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying organizational linkages to publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how organizational consequences 'link' the organization to other systems—publics and other organizations—in the environment; identifying interpenetrating systems, determining which are most likely to upset equilibrium, and planning communications with those systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical three-step management role: (1) identify interpenetrating systems, (2) determine which are likely to upset the equilibrium, (3) plan communication programs with those systems so movements toward a new equilibrium are smooth. Use consequences (organization has consequences on others or vice versa) to find linked systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: Linkages with organizations and social groups that provide the authority and control the resources that enable the organization to exist (e.g., boards of directors, stockholders, legislative bodies, regulators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: government regulators, Congress, state legislators, boards of directors, stockholders. Explains why organizations need government relations, public affairs, and stockholder relations programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional linkages (input and output)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linkages with organizations or publics that provide inputs to or use outputs from the organization; divided into input linkages (suppliers, employees/unions, regulators that provide inputs) and output linkages (dealers, consumers, other organizations that use outputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Input linkages prompt programs such as employee relations, labor relations, supplier relations. Output linkages prompt consumer relations and relations with organizations that use the organization's products or services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: Linkages with organizations that face similar problems or share similar values (e.g., other universities, industry associations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative linkages explain the need for associations and member relations; PR work here focuses on facilitating communication among member organizations to attack common problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffused linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: Linkages with elements in society that cannot be clearly identified by membership in formal organizations — diffused publics that arise when the organization has consequences on people outside the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes community, environmental, and minority publics; media relations is important because media inform diffused publics and help bring them into existence. Organizations often develop environmental relations, minority relations, community relations, and media relations programs to address diffused linkages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using linkage concepts to plan and justify PR programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the taxonomy of linkages (enabling, functional, normative, diffused) to determine which publics and linked organizations an organization should communicate with and to justify specific PR programs to top management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a state university has enabling (legislature), input functional (faculty, students), output functional (employers), normative (other universities), and diffused (community, sports fans) linkages — each suggests specific PR programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary personnel as communicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that organizations contact linked systems through boundary personnel—employees who have as much contact outside the organization as inside (e.g., PR people, salesmen, service representatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners are boundary personnel but may not handle all linkages; other boundary personnel (e.g., president, VP, sales) may communicate with enabling linkages and be assisted by PR staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public (Blumer definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public is a group of people who: (1) are confronted by an issue, (2) are divided in their ideas as to how to meet the issue, (3) engage in discussion over the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with 'mass'—polls measure mass opinion not opinions of publics; publics are homogeneous around a common problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public (Dewey definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public is a group of people who: (1) face a similar problem, (2) recognize that the problem exists, (3) organize to do something about the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects to the behavioral molecule (detect → construct/define/select/confirm → behave); if members pass through these stages they become active publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences create publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics form when organizational consequences affect people outside the organization — those consequences create problems that people detect and around which publics arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a polluting steel mill creates an air-pollution public among those affected who detect the problem and may organize to confront the mill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of publics (nonpublic, latent, aware, active)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify groups by the three Dewey conditions: nonpublic (none apply), latent public (face problem but do not detect it), aware public (recognize the problem), active public (organize to act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category requires different PR objectives and strategies; determine which category a group falls into via research to design appropriate communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating demographic categories as publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate publics with broad demographic categories (e.g., the elderly, women, blacks, urban dwellers) because such categories may include many publics or none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publics are defined by a common problem or consequence, not merely shared demographics or media reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'general public' as a target
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of communicating to the 'general public' is a logical impossibility because publics are always specific and have a common problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR planning should identify specific publics linked by consequences rather than a vague general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: don't wait until publics are active
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with latent or aware publics before they become active; waiting to act until publics are active is a mistake because active publics are harder to influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An active public enters the behave segment and selectively seeks information that reinforces its decision (cognitive-dissonance effects). Early accommodation or communication with aware publics can prevent escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active publics are hard to persuade (selective exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active publics selectively seek and retain information that reinforces the choice they have already made and are unlikely to be open to the same information they sought earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To influence an active public the organization must show that new or worse consequences exist or that prior remedies produced worse outcomes; otherwise persuasion is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and cohesion affect public activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, cohesive publics are more likely to become active and effective adversaries; large, diffuse publics seldom move from aware to active because of free-rider dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Olson's logic: in large groups individuals expect others to act, reducing incentives to mobilize; focus resources on small cohesive publics when threat is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active publics define organizational social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Active publics articulate problems to media and enabling linkages and thereby define what counts as socially responsible behavior for the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate with aware publics to influence the definition of social responsibility before active publics set the public agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational Theory — independent variable: problem recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem recognition is the extent to which people perceive that something needs to be done about a situation (detect segment of the behavioral molecule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring problem recognition helps predict whether people will communicate about a consequence and whether they will belong to a public. It explains active information-seeking behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational Theory — independent variable: constraint recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraint recognition refers to perceptions of obstacles or limits that inhibit action (mentioned as one of the three independent variables in Grunig's theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraint recognition helps explain when people will act or not; it reduces likelihood of information seeking and behavior even when problem recognition is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational Theory — independent variable: level of involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of involvement indicates how personally relevant or important the issue is to individuals; higher involvement increases the likelihood of active communication and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure involvement to predict whether a public will be latent, aware, or active; involvement interacts with problem and constraint recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent behaviors — information seeking (active) vs information processing (passive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active communication behavior (information seeking) is when people look for and try to understand information; passive behavior (information processing) is when people process information that comes to them without seeking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seeking publics become aware and are more likely to use information to plan behavior; passive processors are less likely to mobilize and less susceptible to some communication effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure variables via survey research to classify publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use survey measures of problem recognition, constraint recognition, and level of involvement (and measures of information seeking/processing) to identify and classify publics and to guide PR strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references Exhibit 7–1 as a tool for measuring these variables; systematic research is necessary to avoid planning for nonpublics or mis-targeting resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify publics within linked organizations (target members, not whole organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an organization is linked to another organization (e.g., a legislature), communicate with the members whose roles or interests cause them to detect the consequences—not with the entire linked organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: within a legislature, focus on members on the education committee or those with constituents concerned about university funding rather than the whole legislative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publics are situational and ephemeral — continuously review
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics change with each consequence; organizations should constantly review organizational consequences and research how people react so PR programs do not aim at publics that no longer exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because attitudes and publics are situational, a different consequence (pollution vs product quality) may produce different publics requiring different objectives and strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common PR errors regarding publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent mistakes include planning PR programs for groups that are not part of a public relations problem, waiting until publics are active, and failing to communicate with aware publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a group is a nonpublic, do not expend PR resources. Failing to counter awareness or to explain the organization's point of view risks letting other sources define the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping PR program types to linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: Different linkages imply standard PR programs: employee relations, labor relations, supplier relations, consumer relations, community relations, environmental relations, minority relations, media relations, association/member relations, government relations/public affairs, stockholder relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linkage classification to decide which programs to prioritize and to explain the rationale to management; programs should be tailored to the linkage and the type of public (latent/aware/active).
